---
title: "Capstone: a game from your research"
subtitle: "One mechanic, one screen, five minutes of play, and the science told honestly."
---

The course ends where the Minus 80 Studios games begin: with something real from research, turned into a short game. Yours will be smaller than *Snail Assassin*, and that's the point. A small game you finish teaches you more than a big one you don't.

## The rules

- **One mechanic.** One verb, used well ([lesson 8](../lessons/08-mechanics.qmd#verbs-goals-obstacles)).
- **One screen** to start. A camera and a bigger world can come later.
- **Five minutes** from opening the page to seeing the end.
- **Honest science.** Every claim the game makes is labelled *Verified*, *Hypothesis* or *Abstraction* ([the field guide](../field-guide/05-tuning-and-design.qmd#the-science-document)).
- **Online.** It's done when someone else can play it from a link ([lesson 10](../lessons/10-ship.qmd#put-it-online)).

## Timeline

| When | What |
|---|---|
| Day 3, 12:15 | Pitch: your index card from [exercise 8.5](../lessons/08-mechanics.qmd#exercises), in two minutes |
| Week 1 | A playable toy: the verb works, nothing else does |
| Week 2 | The goal, the obstacle and the one choice. A tuning file. First playtest with three people |
| Week 3 | Feedback and polish. The science file. Deployed |
| Lab meeting | Everyone plays everyone's game |

## Start from

Either the empty starter, or the finished game if your idea is close to *Cold Chain*'s shape (walk somewhere, carry something, avoid something):

```bash
cp -r starter my-capstone          # a blank scene
cp -r stopping-points/stopE my-capstone   # all five scenes, tuning, touch, saves
```

Then make it its own repository, so it can be deployed on its own:

```bash
cd my-capstone
git init
npm install
npm run dev
```

## Two files before any code

Put these at the top of your project. Fill them in before you write the game, and keep them up to date as it changes.

**`DESIGN.md`**

```markdown
# <Title>

One sentence: what you do, and why it matters.

## Verb
## Goal
## Obstacle
## Core loop
1.
2.
3.

## The choice
What's worth a risk, and what does it cost?

## Target experience
How should it feel? (Tense? Calm? Frantic? Curious?)

## Still deciding (proposals)
```

**`SCIENCE.md`**

```markdown
# The science in <Title>

Labels: Verified = stated in a cited source · Hypothesis = proposed by the authors · Abstraction = our invention

| What the game shows | Label | Source | What we simplified |
|---|---|---|---|
|  |  |  |  |

## What players should leave knowing
## What we got wrong on purpose, and why
```

## Example pitches

To show the scale, not to copy. Each is one verb, one screen, five minutes.

::: {.cards}
::: {}
**Loop Extruder**

*Slide* a cohesin ring along a strand of DNA. Stop at a CTCF site that faces the right way to lock in a loop. Other proteins block the path; the ring falls off if you're too slow. *Simplified: one dimension, one ring, invented speeds.*
:::

::: {}
**Cut & Tag**

*Steer* a tethered enzyme to the one histone mark that matters among hundreds that don't. Cut in the wrong place and the background rises. *Simplified: a single nucleus, an exaggerated signal.*
:::

::: {}
**Torpor**

*Ration* body heat through a winter. Rousing costs energy but clears damage; staying cold saves fuel but builds up risk. *Simplified: one animal, a handful of variables, game-time days.*
:::

::: {}
**Gut Feeling**

*Route* signals through the enteric nervous system so a meal moves along at the right pace. Too fast or too slow, and it backs up. *Simplified: a handful of neurons, one reflex.*
:::
:::

## Playtesting

Three people, who haven't seen the game, one at a time ([*Snail Assassin*'s playtesting notes](../field-guide/07-grown-up.qmd#the-docs-folder) are a good model):

1. Give them the link and say only "play however you like".
2. Watch without talking. Note where they hesitate, misunderstand, or smile.
3. Afterwards, ask: *What were you trying to do? What was the most frustrating moment? What did you learn about the science?*

If two of three people misunderstand the same thing, it's the game, not them.

## Done enough to share

- [ ] Someone who's never seen it can start playing without you explaining anything.
- [ ] There's a way to win, a way to lose (or a score), and a way to play again.
- [ ] Every balance number is in one tuning file.
- [ ] `SCIENCE.md` labels every claim, with sources.
- [ ] It works on a phone, or the page says it needs a keyboard.
- [ ] Sound can be turned off, and so can screen shake.
- [ ] It's online, with `base: './'`, from a GitHub Actions workflow.
- [ ] Three people have played it, and you changed something because of what you saw.
